5192.prule: In a sesquisyllabic word the stress falls on the main (major) syllable, which is the last syllable; the one or two minor syllables that precede it (a CV presyllable, a presyllabic nasal, or two CV presyllables) are unstressed and phonologically reduced. 5194.dq: 10. Accent d'intensité sur la syllabe du radical (Ainsi en Zone B.)
5194.dloc: Labaere 2001, p. 172, section 'I. Caractéristiques communes à la Zone C', item 10, translating Guthrie 1948: 36-39; zone framing on pp. 164-165. Motingea 2001: sec. 2.4 'Tons' pp. 280-284 and 2.5 'Syllabe' p. 284.
5194.prule: Stress accent ('accent d'intensité') on the syllable of the radical (root), i.e. the stem-initial syllable, with prefixes and suffixes unstressed by implication. Stated by Guthrie 1948 as a feature common to all of Bantu Zone C ('huit groupes qui contiennent environ quarante langues'; Sengele is C33) and to Zone B; not a statement about Sengele in particular. Lexical tone on radical and suffixes co-exists (item 11).
5194.srule: Not mentioned in Guthrie 1948: 36-39 (Zone C common characteristics, items 1-13, read in Labaere's 2001 French translation, Annales Aequatoria 22: 164-173); the Sengele-specific phonology, Motingea 2001 sec. 2.4-2.5 (Annales Aequatoria 22: 280-284), describes tone only and does not discuss stress at all.

tn.quote: Il existe deux catégories de tons: tons simples et tons complexes. Les tons simples sont le ton bas et le ton haut, représentés respectivement ici par l’absence de tout signe et par l’accent aigu. ... Les tons complexes sont les tons doubles montant et descendant ainsi que les tons triples montant-descendant et descendant-montant. ... Comme ailleurs en bantou, les tons en kɛmbélɔ ont une double valeur: lexicale et grammaticale.
tn.translation: There are two categories of tones: simple tones and complex tones. The simple tones are the low tone and the high tone, represented here respectively by the absence of any sign and by the acute accent. ... The complex tones are the double tones, rising and falling, as well as the triple tones, rising-falling and falling-rising. ... As elsewhere in Bantu, the tones in kɛmbélɔ have a double value: lexical and grammatical.

5199.prule: No word-stress rule stated for Teda. The chapter reports (after Le Cœur 1956) that Teda, unlike Kanuri, has no elaborate tonal system and that Le Cœur leaves tone unmarked; for Tubu (Lukas's southern/Kashirda material) it reports important but fluctuating tone with lexical and grammatical uses, High/Low/Rising tones, and a strong stress accent ('Akzent (Druck)') that Lukas mentions but does not illustrate and that may affect tones; vowel length in Teda-Tubu is 'perhaps associated with stress'. Where stress falls in the word is not stated by Tucker & Bryan, nor by Lukas as quoted in Dybo 1995:239 ('In welcher Weise der Akzent rhythmisch im Satz verteilt wird, bedarf näherer Untersuchung'), and Dybo 1995:240 states that Lukas accents every example 'не давая, впрочем, какого-либо общего правила, которое определяло бы место ударения в словоформе' (without, however, giving any general rule that would fix the place of stress in the word-form).

5201.dq: En la jerarquía prosódica del cuicateco, la formación de la palabra fonológica tiene como requerimiento que el pie métrico tenga un contenido mínimo de dos moras y que el acento se fije en la segunda mora de derecha a izquierda según la exposición de Martínez y Mendoza (2016). (p. 47) — stress is assigned in the formation of the phonological word ('palabra fonológica', example (1) p. 19 lists 'as…
5201.dloc: sec. 2.4 p. 47; with example (1) p. 19 (sec. 1.3, 'palabra fonológica... asignación de acento') and sec. 6.4 p. 146 ('los radicales').
5201.heavy: A syllable containing the second mora from the right edge of the root; heaviness = a long (bimoraic) vowel (San Giacomo 2017 p. 97 [βi⁴ˈkuː³] 'fiesta', [jų³ˈðuː⁴] 'llano' vs [ˈka²ka²] 'papel', [ˈjuː⁴ði⁴] 'elote'; San Giacomo 2025 p. 46 [ðu³ˈtuː³⁴] 'hill': 'it falls on the last syllable of the word 'hill' because the vowel is long and the second mora, counted from the right to the left, is found in this syllable'). The mora is the tone-bearing unit ('En cuicateco la unidad portadora de tono es la mora', p. 47); the phonological word requires a foot of at least two moras ('un contenido mínimo de dos moras', p. 47), so monosyllabic roots lengthen (ˈnãː 'cara' p. 19; Teotilálpam [ˈⁿdoː⁴²⁴] 'vena' Cuadro 6.4, [ˈtʃãː⁴] 'lune' Cuadro 6.5). Codas: the thesis's 'prohibición de coda' (p. 145) is stated for the colonial Confessonario variety only ('Las sílabas fonológicas del cuicateco del Confessonario podían ser CV o V... iii) la prohibición de coda'); present-day varieties have VC/CVC syllables (San Giacomo 2017 p. 97: 'permite dos consonantes asignadas al onset y una en coda... (Ariano 2016): V, VC, CV, CCV y CVC'; San Giacomo 2025 p. 46 citing Ariano 2023; Mendoza's Teotilálpam [ˈsnĩŋ³⁴] ~ [ˈsⁿdẽŋ³⁴] 'sombrero', Cuadro 6.4 p. 125, a stressed CVC monosyllable printed without a length mark where Tepeuxila [ˈsⁿdĩː⁴³⁴] and Reyes Pápalo [ˈsnĩː³²³] have long vowels). Whether a coda consonant carries a mora is unstated in every source read, so CVC weight is neither asserted nor excluded. Whether a laryngeal feature (CVʔ) carries a mora is left open for the colonial variety (p. 146: 'ya sea con valor de una mora o, como sucede en algunas realizaciones actuales, entre la transición moraica').
5201.dflt: Penultimate syllable of the root (the first syllable of a disyllabic short-vowelled root: [ˈka²ka²] 'papel', ˈkʷekuð); a monosyllabic root is lengthened to two moras and stressed (ˈnãː 'cara').
5201.prule: Weight-sensitive, non-contrastive: a moraic trochee at the right edge of the root. Stress falls on the syllable that contains the second mora counting from the right edge of the root ('la sílaba de la segunda mora a partir del linde derecho [de] los radicales'; 'el acento se fije en la segunda mora de derecha a izquierda'). A root whose final syllable has a long (bimoraic) vowel is stressed on that final syllable; a root with short vowels is stressed on its penultimate syllable; monosyllabic roots are lengthened to satisfy the two-mora minimum of the phonological word and carry the stress (p. 19: nã 'cara' -> ˈnãː; ku+eku+ði 'IRRE-llorar=2PS' -> ˈkʷekuð). Prefixes and enclitics lie outside the counting domain (corpus forms a-ti-ˈβaʔ=ði, tʃe-noɣiˈβiʔ=ði, ˈβiʔ=ði). Stated for 'las variedades actuales de cuicateco' in general; illustrated by San Giacomo 2017 for San Juan Tepeuxila: [βi⁴ˈkuː³] 'fiesta', [jų³ˈðuː⁴] 'llano' (final long vowel, final stress) vs [ˈka²ka²] 'papel', [ˈjuː⁴ði⁴] 'elote'.
5201.srule: Not mentioned in Mendoza Hernández 2023 (sec. 6.4 'Características prosódicas' pp. 145-146, sec. 2.4 p. 47, sec. 1.3 pp. 19-20 read): the thesis describes a single stress per root (a moraic trochee at the right edge of the root) and says nothing about secondary or rhythmic stress; the cross-check sources for San Juan Tepeuxila (San Giacomo 2017 pp. 97-98; San Giacomo 2025 p. 46) are likewise silent.

The thesis analyses the colonial Confessonario and compares it with present-day speech from 8 communities in INALI's three variants: centro (Santos Reyes Pápalo, San Juan Tepeuxila, San Lorenzo Pápalo, San Sebastián Tlacolula), norte…
5201.exq_: La asignación del acento suele coincidir con la sílaba prominente en palabras bisilábicas o de mayor extensión. (p. 146) — the only hedge; it concerns the coincidence of the stressed syllable with the 'sílaba prominente' (the syllable licensing the most oppositions), not exceptions to the mora rule…
5201.tone: Cuicatec is tonal ('el cuicateco es tonal', p. 47); the tone-bearing unit is the mora, and tones associate one-to-one or one-to-many with moras (p. 47, citing Needham & Davis 1946 and San Giacomo 2017: four level, five contour, three complex tones for Tepeuxila). Stress is described independently of tone as the position licensing the most segmental oppositions, with intensity and duration as correlates (p. 146). No pitch-accent analysis.

tn.quote: Al igual que los otros integrantes de la familia otomangue, el cuicateco es tonal. … En cuicateco la unidad portadora de tono es la mora (Needham y Davis 1946 y San Giacomo 2017); y su asociación ocurre entre un tono y una mora, o bien entre un tono y varias moras. … De acuerdo con los estudios publicados el paradigma de tonos varía entre los tres y cuatro registros de nivel. … Anderson y Concepción (1983), también para Santa María, y San Giacomo (2017) para Tepeuxila han hallado cuatro alturas tonales; en este último San Giacomo propone además cinco patrones de contorno y 3 patrones complejos
tn.translation: Like the other members of the Otomanguean family, Cuicatec is tonal. … In Cuicatec the tone-bearing unit is the mora (Needham & Davis 1946; San Giacomo 2017), and association holds between one tone and one mora, or between one tone and several moras. … According to the published studies the tone paradigm varies between three and four level registers. … Anderson & Concepción (1983), also for Santa María, and San Giacomo (2017) for Tepeuxila have found four tone heights; in the latter San Giacomo further proposes five contour patterns and 3 complex patterns

tn.note: Tonal; the mora bears tone. Varieties: 3 or 4 level tones; Tepeuxila 4 level, 5 contour, 3 complex (12). A bare high tone can mark 1st person. Stress is separate: 2nd mora from the root's right edge.

5201.cfw: Mendoza Hernández (2023), who collected data in eight Cuicatec communities including the Teutila towns of San Pedro Teutila, Santa María Tlalixtac and San Andrés Teotilálpam, and San Giacomo (2017, 2025) for San Juan Tepeuxila place stress on the syllable that holds the second mora counted from the right edge of the root, while the older Pápalo descriptions (Anderson & Concepción Roque 1983; Needham & Davis 1946) speak of a light stress at the beginning of the root, which picks out the same syllable in ordinary CVCV and CVː roots, so the sources differ in formulation rather than in where stress falls; no published description treats the stress of Teutila Cuicatec on its own.

qtr.text: [p.57] Apart from a few languages such as Swahili, almost all Bantu languages are tone languages, and most have phonological tone (Kisseberth and Odden 2003: 59). Like the great majority of Bantu languages, Bende has distinctive tone that differentiates meaning. ... [p.59] There are three stem/root tonal types, called H(igh), L(ow) and 0 type: H type begins with H, L type begins with L, and in the 0 type the penultimate syllable is H and the final syllable L again. Most loanwords are realised as 0 type. ... Tone rule 1, basic realised tones of stems/roots [1σ 2σ 3σ 4σ+]: H type H HH HHH HHHH …

5202.dq: No stress at any level is described. The tonal melody is computed over the word: [p.59] 語幹ないし語根ごとに決められた声調型で実現されるべき H ないし L は, 語全体の音節数によって H や L の声調を 1 つずつ音節に結びつけられないことがある. そうした場合, 1 音節上で HL が F, LH が R で実現される.
5202.dloc: p.59 (第3章 声調, §1.2 声調の種類, 声調型), p.3
5202.prule: No stress rule is stated. The thesis describes a lexical tone system: each noun stem / verb root belongs to one of three tonal types (H, L, 0) and the surface tones H/L/F/R are assigned by tonal type and the word's syllable count (声調規則 1: H type H/HH/HHH/HHHH, L type R/LH/LHH/LHHH, 0 type R/RL(or HL)/LHL/LLHL; most loans are 0 type).
5202.quote: [p.57] Swahili 語など少数の言語を除き, ほとんどの Bantu 諸語は声調言語で, その多くが音韻的声調を持つ(Kisseberth and Odden 2003: 59). ベンデ語も大多数の Bantu 諸語と同様, 意味の区別に弁別的な声調を持つ. ... [p.59] 語幹ないし語根の声調型には 3 種類あり, それぞれ H(igh) 型, L(ow) 型, 0 型と呼ぶことにする. H 型は語幹ないし語根が H で始まるもの, L 型は語幹ないし語根が L で始まるもの, 0 型は後ろから 2 番目の音節が H となり最終音節は再び L となるものである. 借用語の多くが 0 型で実現される. ... 声調規則 1 語幹, 語根の基本的な実現声調 [1σ 2σ 3σ 4σ以上 例(2σ語根)]: H 型 H HH HHH HHHH -bhá.mbá (皮を)張る; L 型 R LH LHH LHHH -bha.ndá 突っつく; 0 型 R RL/HL LHL LLHL -soó.ka 降りる.
5202.loc: p.57 (第3章 声調, §1 ベンデ語声調の特徴) and p.59 (§1.2 声調の種類, 声調型; 声調規則 1); also p.269 (終章 §2 方言差), p.7 (序章 §1.5 + fn.3), p.20 (第1章, (3) トングウェ語の特徴, after Guthrie 1967-71 vol.2: 47). TUFS repository scans (image-only): pp.1, 3; p.3; p.7; p.4.
5202.idn: The cited thesis is a description of Bende (Guthrie F.12; Glottolog bend1258, a separate catalog record) from fieldwork in Mpanda District. It bears on Tongwe (F.11) through the author's explicit statement that Bende and Tongwe are two dialects of one language, identical 'including tone' (p.269), which rests on her…
5202.exq_: No stress rule, so no stress exceptions. On the tone rule: [p.59] 音節構造や統語構造により異形があるが, 異形については後述する. [p.59] 借用語の多くが 0 型で実現される.
5202.tone: Distinctive lexical tone ([p.57] minimal pairs íikálá 'clawless otter' vs íikalá 'charcoal', lúsángá 'flower' vs lúsangá 'healer's maracas', úughwě 'you' vs uúghwe 'this (proximal demonstrative)'; verbs kúfúlá / kúfulá / kufuúla). Surface tones H, L, F, R realised on short-vowel, long-vowel, diphthong and glide+vowel syllables alike (table (4), p.59). Three stem/root tonal types H, L, 0 with melodies fixed by syllable count (声調規則 1). Tongwe-specific tone evidence in the thesis: Guthrie's characterisation of F.11 Tongwe, quoted on p.20 under '(3) トングウェ語の特徴': 'Tones: Fully distinctive, but opaque'; Guthrie's zone-F feature 16 on the same page: 'F.33 (Laŋgi)を除き, すべての言語で語彙的声調が用いられる. 声調によって時制が区別される例が多い.'; and the tone-marked Tongwe forms in the p.269 dialect-difference table (íibhíngá, mábhíngá; síinyú, fíinyú; mumbáti, mimbáti; muunyú; kabhěnga, tubhěnga; síkólé, fíkólé). 5203.prule: Only emphatic / focus stress is described, at the level of the utterance: 'strong stress' (प्रबल बल) falls on whichever word of the sentence answers the question under discussion (baṇḍi vāvrāt neli: stress on vāvrāt 'to the field' answering 'where?', on baṇḍi 'cart' answering 'what?'); 'extra-strong stress' (अतिप्रबल बल) falls on the particular syllable that carries a contrast (on the ā of āplyā 'our own', not somebody else's); 'clipped stress' (तुटक बल) gives 'only / exactly' readings; 'prolonged stress' (विलंबित बल) marks calls and intensification. No rule for the position of word stress is given, and word stress is neither described nor denied; so the record is phrase-level prominence only, word-level placement unreported.

5209.dq: p.219 fn.144: "'Dans la plupart des langues, cette unité accentuelle est ce qu'on appelle couramment le mot' (Cf. Martinet, A., 1980, Éléments de linguistique générale, p. 89). Nous avons préféré utiliser le terme d'unité accentuelle au lieu de celui de 'mot phonologique' pour éviter de recourir à une terminologique qui pourrait interférer avec la morphologie ou la syntaxe." (p.159 §1.3.3: 'L'uni…
5209.prule: Stress (accent) is predictable and non-distinctive: it falls on the first syllable of the accentogenic element of the accentual unit, i.e. the first syllable of the radical (root/stem). Proclitic syllables cannot bear stress: the class prefix ha(n)-, a syllabic nasal, any syllable whose nucleus is schwa (e.g. the class prefix kə-), and proclitic pronouns. Hence surface stress is on the first syllable of the unit unless a proclitic precedes, in which case it is on the second. Examples (p.159): ['wɔ:mna] 'eat!', [ha'la:nte] 'man', [kə'demat] 'tongue (organ)' vs ['demat] 'tongues', [ń'kpa:s ('ma:le)] 'I cultivated rice', [(ha'la:nte) han'da:ŋ] 'a big man', [ha'bi:k 'bit.ń] 'he saw a dog'. Stress is realised as extra intensity and, to some extent, extra pitch (p.158).
5209.srule: In accentual units of more than three syllables an 'echo' accent, comparable to a secondary stress, falls on the penultimate syllable: [fń'racˌta:nde] 'flirt' (p.159: "Dans les unités accentuelles de plus de trois syllabes, on peut noter un écho d'accent assimilable à un accent secondaire... sur l'avant dernière syllabe.").
5209.quote: p.158: "La place de l'accent est prévisible. En règle générale, l'accent porte sur la première syllabe de l'unité accentuelle, sauf lorsque celle-ci est un élément proclitique. La syllabe ha(n)-, la nasale syllabique Ń et une syllabe dont la voyelle [ə] est le noyau constituent des éléments clitiques. Leur présence implique que l'accent se porte sur la deuxième syllabe." ... p.166: "La place de celui-ci n'assume aucune fonction distinctive; l'accent occupe une place déterminée dans l'unité accentuelle: il frappe la première syllabe de l'élément accentogène, en l'occurrence le radical. De ce f…
5209.loc: Tome I, Ch. I §1.3 'Phonétique supra-segmentale: l'accent', §1.3.2 'Place de l'accent' p.158 and p.159 (restatement, examples, echo accent, §1.3.3 'Unité accentuelle', fn.104); Ch. II p.166 (radical-initial, non-distinctive); pp.168-169 (tonal hypothesis rejected); §2.5.3.1 p.219 fn.144 (accentual unit = phonological word), p.220 (max five syllables); §2.6.2 p.251 (demarcative function). page numbers are in the page header; the on-file locator's pp. 159-160/167/252 are these same passages numbered one page too high.
5209.idn: Mbodj describes balante so:fa, which he presents as a component of the kənto:he (Kantohe) dialect, 'celui des Balantes dont le territoire est entièrement situé dans la partie nord de la Guinée-Bissau'; §0.2.2 (p.15) divides kənto:he into two sub-dialects, so:fa and fac. His field surveys were in the Oio and Cacheu regions, with informants from those regions living in Bissau, Canchungo, Ncan and Mbuti, and initial work with a Balanta speaker in Dakar (Intro §0.4.1, p.17). Glottolog lists Kantohe as a dialect of Balanta-Kentohe (bala1301); the variety is not Balanta-Ganja (bala1302).
5209.exq_: p.159: "Autrement dit, l'accent frappe toujours la première syllabe de l'élément accentogène ou la deuxième syllabe de l'unité accentuelle lorsque la première est une syllabe proclitique comme indiqué ci-dessus."
5209.tone: The author explicitly rejects a tonal analysis for Balanta Sofa (pp. 168-169): no tonal minimal pairs were found, the H/L word melodies expected under a two-tone hypothesis do not occur, and no grammatical function of tone was identified; the raised pitch on the stressed radical-initial syllable and the 'pont tonal' between intonation groups are treated as phonetic correlates of accent/intonation ('les réalisations tonales doivent être considérées comme des phénomènes phonétiques'). Only primary accent is marked in phonetic transcriptions. NB the sister language Balanta-Ganja (bala1302) is analysed as tonal (H vs L) by Creissels 2024 / Creissels & Biaye 2016; that is a different language under Glottolog and a different author's analysis, not a conflict for bala1301.

contra.head: A handbook chapter says Bhatise has interacting tones and stress accents, not the Indus Kohistani pitch accent
contra.detail: One sentence in a survey chapter on Indic dialectology, with no source given for it (the chapter's reference list has no Bateri or Indus Kohistani work; Zoller appears only for 1988 Bangani, Baart 1997 for Kalam Kohistani). It states, p. 436: 'Bhatise is on the east bank of the Indus opposite Besham. Instead of the pitch accent system of other varieties of Indus Kohistani, Bhatise has a complex system of interacting tones and stress accents.' This runs against the entry's pitch-accent classification, which rests on Zoller 2005 (pp. 22-23: B lemmata marked rising/falling but 'never checked with the speech analyzer'; B 'expected' to be like J) and against Strand's first-hand description of tw…

5210.dq: In case of the B words, many of the have been marked either with the rising or the falling accent. ... (p. 26, rule 2) Each morpheme contains one syllable either with a rising or a falling accent.
5210.prule: Lexical pitch accent (as transcribed, unanalysed): each Bateri word in the dictionary carries one accented syllable, marked rising (acute) or falling (grave), whose position varies from lexeme to lexeme (initial in áṅgo 'courtyard', àmbūr 'pliers'; final in aṅgùi 'finger', axòr 'hay', adràk 'ginger', ará 'saw'); no rule predicting the place of the accent is given. Zoller expects the B system to be 'quite similar' to the Jijali Indus Kohistani system (two contrastive accent contours, rising vs falling; 'each morpheme contains one syllable either with a rising or a falling accent'; contour contrast neutralised on short vowels in polysyllables), but states that the B rising/falling marking was never checked instrumentally.
5210.srule: None stated for Bateri. (For J compounds Zoller marks a dominant nucleus accent with the other accent at a lower level, p. 28; not stated for B.)
5210.quote: The lemmata from B and G have not been analyzed in this way. This means the following: in the majority of cases, accent marking of the G words only indicates the place of the accent. ... In case of the B words, many of the [sic] have been marked either with the rising or the falling accent. This marking, however, was never checked with the speech analyzer. However, since B and G appear to have similar cases of accent shift under specific conditions (a synopsis of the rules for J is given below in section 2.3.), it is to be expected that the accent systems of B and G are quite similar to those…
5210.loc: Ch. 2 'Technical aspects of the dictionary', sec. 2 'On phonology and tonology', pp. 22-23; sec. 3 'Some pitch accent rules', p. 26 rules 1-2; Ch. 1 sec. 1.5 'Own research', pp. 6-7 (B and G accent systems: 'It was not possible to analyze their accent systems with the speech analyzer'); identity p. 1 and abbreviation list p. 41 'B = Bhat.ise (also called Bat.er.a)'; '(B)'-tagged lemmata passim.
5210.tone: Zoller treats Bateri (B) as having a pitch accent system of the Indus Kohistani/Shina kind: one accented syllable per morpheme/word with a rising vs falling contour contrast; B differs tonetically from J by a shorter peak-delay, so the accent mark is often written on the consonant preceding the tone-bearing vowel (p. 23, p. 26 rule 1). He states explicitly that the B accent system 'was never checked with the speech analyzer' and that only J 'has been completely phonologized and tonologized' (p. 22); the similarity to J is his expectation ('it is to be expected'), not a demonstrated result. No word-stress rule separate from the accent is described.

5211.dq: III. The most noteworthy difference in accent exists among words of two syllables, some having an even stress on both syllables, and some having a real accent on the first. (p. 15; word accent; the 'stress' of pp. 54 and 145 is sentence emphasis on an object / a statement, treated in the syntax)
5211.prule: No Bviri-specific accent placement rule beyond remark V. Santandrea 1961 treats Ndogo, Sere, Tagbu, Bai and Bviri together; sec. 4 'Accent' gives, 'especially of Ndogo', 'suggestions (I shall not call them rules)': I. monosyllables unproblematic; II. 'a good few' polysyllables are compounds of monosyllables, 'each one of which must have its own accent duly stressed' ('denje SPEAK, vvindii REPAIR, tokponje QUARREL, kuri); III. disyllables have either 'an even stress on both syllables' or 'a real accent on the first', the latter being words with l, r, n in the second syllable (toro, kátá, mele, ngele, kele, téné, sènè, koro, moro), and where « r » is concerned the second syllable is often lost (mbòro = mbòò, kóró = kóó); IV. reduplicated disyllables accent syllables 1 and 3; p. 29: 'the accent usually lies on the first syllable of dissyllables'. Remark V extends this to Bviri: 'Most of the remarks made for Ndogo hold good', adding only that Bviri often drops a final vowel (esp. -i after n) in compounds (kon(i), son(i) - kuukon, sonson) and in words of [foreign] origin (del(i) GOAT, uton(i) HYENA). The language is tonal (sec. 5 'Tone', pp. 16-33; Wáũ 2020: three level tones).
5211.srule: None stated as such. In compounds each monosyllabic component 'must have its own accent duly stressed'; in reduplicated disyllables 'accents lie on the first and third syllables' (p. 29; lebelebe, reperepe, kacakaca), exception mbulambula with the accent on the second syllable (p. 15 IV b).

(b) occasionally the opposite phenomenon is met with, viz. the accent lies on the second syllable, though it cont…
5211.tone: Tone is the word-prosodic system. Santandrea 1961 sec. 5 'TONE' occupies pp. 16-33: p. 17 '... above (low, mid, high, very high) may well represent, as already hinted...'; p. 29 'reduplication is as a rule « sameness » of tones throughout the whole word'; pp. 25/28 higher tone on the first component in 'i' + reduplication. Wáũ 2020 p. 24 (open text, consulted again): 'In Viri, there are three tone levels, namely, high (H), low (L) and mid (M). The mid tone in Viri is often left unmarked.... Viri tone has both grammatical and lexical functions.' Bilal 2004 (OPSL 9: 180) likewise three level tones, lexical and grammatical. Neither modern source mentions stress or accent; Santandrea's accent remarks are offered as pronunciation 'suggestions', not rules.

tn.quote: Since all tones occur at one of three levels, Viri is classified as a register tone language. If a contour tone occurs in a word it is composed of two different tones, and there are also two vowels. In Viri, there are three tone levels, namely, high (H), low (L) and mid (M). The mid tone in Viri is often left unmarked. ... This illustrates that Viri tone has both grammatical and lexical functions.

tn.note: Three level tones H, M, L, lexical and grammatical (e.g. ká 'is' vs kà 'was'); surface contours are two tones on two vowels; Bilal 2004 agrees; nothing on stress; Santandrea 1961 unobtainable in full.

Valenzuela 2011: 278 says stress is not phonological (non-contrastive) in Cahuapanan ('las lenguas cahuapana' = Jebero and Chayahuita) but gives a placement rule only for Jebero. 5214.dq: A further difference is that for some words, Kumalu, Mumengtein, and Pelenkwa have a different stress pattern, so that not only does the initial syllable have a full vowel, but it also receives stress.
5214.prule: None stated for Dambi. The survey's only stress sentence characterises Patep (initial unstressed syllables always have schwa) and names Kumalu, Mumengtein and Pelenkwa as having, for some words, a different pattern in which a full-vowelled initial syllable is stressed; Dambi is not named and no rule is given for it. Appendix B (pp. 16-27) marks stress with ' on the Dambi (Zoo village) citation forms without comment, and the marks fall on different syllables: second-syllable stress in nə'lu 'nose', ɓa'mbo 'stomach', la'ndag 'stone', ka'ndaŋk 'big', nə'ɓu 'tooth', nə'ma 'hand', ɓa'ga 'foot', ndɛ'nduk 'moon', ɓə'linek 'star', ɓə'wɛɓ 'ashes'; initial stress in 'mɛnik 'bird', 'mao 'man', 'nɔu 'dog', 'ninya 'ear', 'ŋgais 'tongue'; two marks in 'nina'ɓi 'skin' and 'lu ka'nsɛk 'head'. No placement rule can be stated from the source without our own analysis of the list.
5214.quote: There seems to be a closer correspondence of vowels between Patep and Kumalu-Dambi-Mumengtein, even though they don't share as many cognates overall. Initial unstressed syllables in Patep always have the vowel schwa [ə]. It appears to be a neutralised vowel, since some of the other dialects have full vowels in that position. A further difference is that for some words, Kumalu, Mumengtein, and Pelenkwa have a different stress pattern, so that not only does the initial syllable have a full vowel, but it also receives stress. Chart F shows other phonological comparisons between the various diale…

5215.dq: While there has been no systematic study of stress in the Kru group as a whole (an exception to this is Innes's (1966) and Luckau's (1975) studies of Grebo stress where it is claimed that stress in Grebo is contrastive), there is a parallel between loss of stress in Neo-Melenesian and the shift from independent word to verbal suffix in Kru.
5215.prule: No word-stress rule stated for Dewoin in any reachable source. Marchese (1986), a comparative Kru grammar whose sample includes first-hand Dewoin data (Welmers and Mortvedt's materials plus her own consultant Bai Boikai of John Town, Bomi), states family-wide that every Kru language has three or four register tones with lexical and grammatical function; her Dewoin examples are tone-marked and Dewoin 'presumptive' pronouns are distinguished by a lengthened low-tone vowel (p. 54). On stress she states that no systematic study exists for Kru as a whole, the only exception being Grebo (Innes 1966, Luckau 1975: contrastive stress).
5215.quote: Kru has both lexical and grammatical tone. Languages have either three or four register tones ... Tone plays an extremely important role in the grammatical systems of the Kru family, making such distinctions as perfective/imperfective aspect, possessive/relative/subject pronouns, definite/indefinite, and sometimes singular/plural. ... [p. 54] in examining the Dewoin verbal system, we note that there is a set of pronouns which Welmers (1977b) describes as "presumptive." These pronouns, characterized by a lengthened low-tone vowel, are used to designate future and customary actions. ... [p. 261…
5215.loc: Marchese 1986: sec. 1.4.1 p. 16; ch. 2 p. 54; ch. 5 (Exbraciation) p. 261 (printed pages; scanned and read).
5215.tone: Tone language by family-level statement (Marchese 1986 p. 16: 'Kru has both lexical and grammatical tone. Languages have either three or four register tones'; Vogler 2017/2024 sec. 2.4 likewise: three registers in Bassa, Klao, Neyo..., four in Grebo, Bete, Vata...). Dewoin's own register count is not stated by either author. Dewoin data in Marchese are tone-marked (e.g. p. 54 ex. 53 from Welmers). Stress/accent: Marchese p. 261 says there has been no systematic study of stress in the Kru group as a whole; Grebo alone has been described (contrastive stress, Innes 1966, Luckau 1975). Nothing on Dewoin stress or accent anywhere in Marchese (whole-book scan by the compilers; pp. 16, 54, 261 re-read here), Vogler, Koelle 1854, Delafosse 1904, Johnston 1906, Thomas 1916.

tn.quote: Kru has both lexical and grammatical tone. Languages have either three or four register tones, which in this study will usually be marked in the following way: in a four-tone system, high tone will be marked by ´, mid-high tone by ', mid tone by ¯, and low tone by `. In three-tone systems, the symbol ´ will mark high, - mid, and ` low. In both three-tone and four-tone languages, mid tone is often unmarked. ... What appear to be contour or modulated tones also occur in several languages. These are interpreted as a combination of two register tones ...

evidence_works.work: Singler 1984, On the underlying representation of contour tones in Wobe (Studies in African Linguistics 15(1): 59-75)
evidence_works.detail: Not about Dewoin; in a historical aside (p. 67) Singler groups Dewoin with Bassa, Krahn and Guere as languages in which 'links have been noted between consonant type and tone', crediting Welmers 1975 ('Dewɔĩ: Some notes and questions after two weeks', UCLA ms., reference list p. 75) for Dewoin, and states the usual pattern: 'Though there are exceptions, the usual pattern is that a voiced consonant in these languages lowers the onset of the following tone.' (p. 67). Secondhand for Dewoin; no register count for Dewoin, no stress content.

evidence_works.work: Marchese 1982, Basic aspectual categories in Proto-Kru (Journal of West African Languages 12(1): 3-23)
evidence_works.detail: Comparative reconstruction of Kru aspect; names Dewoin among the Western languages with an unmarked perfective and states, sec. 3.1 (printed p. 6): 'The unmarked perfective occurs in many Western languages including Dewoin, Klao, Grebo, Krahn, Wobé and Nyabwa. In these languages tonal differences on the verb have nothing to do with aspect; they merely reflect lexical tone.' The Dewoin material is credited to Welmers 1977 ('Welmers (1977) reports that in Dewoin imperfective actions are signalled by a periphrastic progressive construction', printed p. 17) and consists of tone-marked 'presumptive' pronoun forms, exx. (31)-(32), printed p. 17 - the same Welmers data that Marchese 1986 p. 54 ex. 53 already gives. No register count for Dewoin, nothing on stress or accent.

5217.dq: Syllable stress of individual words does not effect the intonation, but the sentence stress over rides both word stress and normal intonation contour. Sentence stress or point of emphasis is always carried by a high pitch.
5217.heavy: Syllables whose nucleus is the low vowel /a/: 'Stress is sometimes related to and predictable by the low vowel /a/'. No statement that /a/ is longer; length is said to follow stress, not to attract it.
5217.dflt: Second syllable in words of more than one syllable ('usually falls on the second syllable'); the source does not explicitly frame this as the no-/a/ case, only as the usual position.
5217.prule: Word stress is non-phonemic (not contrastive). In words of more than one syllable it usually falls on the second syllable; it is sometimes instead related to and predictable by the presence of the low vowel /a/ (i.e. a syllable with /a/ can carry the stress). Non-contrastive vowel length accompanies the stressed syllable. No lexical tone; pitch functions only as intonation, and sentence stress (high pitch) overrides word stress.

5219.dq: Phonétiquement, la voyelle de toute syllabe pré-finale se réalise semi-longue en hunde. (Mateene does not say whether 'pré-finale' is counted in the word or the utterance; his examples are isolation words. Bastin 2003:504 locates the Hunde penultimate length 'at the end of an utterance or elicitation forms'. No stress of any domain is described, hence UNSTATED for stress.)
5219.prule: No word stress is stated. Hunde is described as a tone language: the Proto-Bantu tones are maintained (H written with an acute, L unmarked; where Greenberg reconstructs H on both syllables of a disyllabic stem, Hunde has H on the first syllable only: n-góko 'poule', mu-kâtsi 'femelle', -kûlu 'âgé', i-ânika, i-hûmula), while the phonological value of vowel quantity is lost; the only non-tonal prominence mentioned is phonetic: the vowel of every pre-final (penultimate) syllable is realized half-long. An independent handbook statement agrees: Bastin 2003:504 (The Bantu Languages ch. 25 §2.1) says that in Hunde 'length is limited to the penultimate vowel at the end of an utterance or elicitation forms: Hunde ìbàlé…; ìbă:lè stone'.
5219.srule: Not applicable; the source describes no secondary or non-tonal prominence other than penultimate half-length.

Phonétiquement, la voyelle de toute syllabe pré-finale se réalise semi-longue en hunde. 3.2 Sur le plan tonologique, les données du H. semblent, dans la majorité des cas, confirmer les recons…
5219.loc: p. 67 (Note préliminaire) and pp. 69-70, §3 'Phonèmes supra-segmentaux', §§3.1-3.2 with footnote 3 (Persée page views T1_67, T1_69, T1_70); the 'semi-longue' sentence is on p. 70.
5219.tone: Mateene 1967 (native-speaker linguist) treats tone as the only distinctive suprasegmental of Hunde (p. 67: PB tones maintained, vowel quantity no longer phonological; §3.2 p. 70: tone correspondences, PB *HH > H on first syllable only) and never uses 'accent' or stress for Hunde; the sole prominence remark is §3.1 'la voyelle de toute syllabe pré-finale se réalise semi-longue' (phonetic penultimate half-lengthening). Philippson 1991 (Thèse d'État, pp. 70, 412-413, 483-485) likewise treats Hunde as a poorly known group-I tone language (HH reduced to HB in isolation forms, data from Mateene 1967) and does not place it in any category of his penultimate-accent typology. Coded like the sister record Nyanga (Kadima 1965): tonal, penultimate lengthening phonetic only.

(3) Le ton haut est noté au moyen d'un accent aigu ('), le ton bas n'est pas noté
tn.translation: On the suprasegmental level, according to the data at our disposal, the tones of Proto-Bantu are maintained in Hunde, whereas the phonological value of vowel quantity seems lost. ... 3.2 On the tonological level, the Hunde data seem, in most cases, to confirm Greenberg's reconstructions. ... where Greenberg reconstructed a high tone on each syllable of certain disyllabic forms, the Hunde correspondences show us only a high tone on the first syllable ... (3) High tone is marked with an acute accent ('), low tone is not marked

tn.note: Brief diachronic sketch (Hunde reflexes of Proto-Bantu): two tones, high (acute) vs low (unmarked), Proto-Bantu tones retained; PB *HH stems show H on the first syllable only. No tone rules described.
